claims.text: Adding a minor amount of Ni to the Cu matrix will cause Ni to segregate to W/Cu interfaces.
Ni segregation will produce a stable, thin, Ni-rich layer on W surfaces at W/Cu boundaries.
The Ni-rich interfacial layer will reduce the interfacial energy between W and Cu.
The Ni-rich interfacial layer will improve Cu wettability on W.
The Ni-rich interfacial layer will strengthen bonding at W/Cu interfaces.
Reduced interfacial energy and improved wetting and bonding will suppress phase separation in the W–Cu composite.
Reduced interfacial energy and improved wetting and bonding will suppress interfacial-void formation.
The Ni-rich interfacial layer will remain stable during thermal cycling.
The Ni-rich interfacial layer will remain stable under irradiation.
Ni addition will produce a denser and more continuous W/Cu interface than in an untreated composite.
Ni addition will reduce W/Cu interfacial void density relative to an untreated composite.
Ni addition will reduce phase separation relative to an untreated W–Cu composite.
Fewer interfacial voids and a more stable interface will improve the composite's overall thermal conductivity.
A Ni-added W–Cu composite will have higher thermal conductivity than an otherwise identically processed untreated W–Cu composite after thermal cycling and irradiation.
The intervention is applicable only when processing permits controlled Ni segregation to W/Cu interfaces.
The intervention is applicable only over service temperatures and irradiation doses at which Ni remains interfacial without forming extensive secondary phases.
